questions.title_en: Chacham Hillel Vs. Chassidic Kabbalah
questions.question:
I heard from my friend Rabbi Botton that Chacham Hillel Shlita has a philosophical difference regarding the way of studying Kabbalah, with the Chassidim. He heard it in a class from a young Chacham but that's all he can tell me.

I don't know exactly what was said but the following do seem to apply:

  1. He wasn't saying that Chassidic learning is fundamentally wrong in and of itself
  2. He was framing it as a preference
  3. It isn't anything to do with the controversy regarding the Baal Shem Tov's use of "non-Vitalian sources".

I don't dare to misquote him, so please understand that this is just third hand "hearsay" and is only provided to help someone who might know respond, but it was something along the lines of him not liking the more philosophical, expansive way of explaining Kabbalah, with lots of deep connections between matters, bechina of this and bechina of that etc, e.g. the way HaRav Morgenstern Shlita teaches.

Can someone please confirm what he thinks about it more precisely, as well as explain it in more detail? Why doesn't he like what he claims to not like? What does he find wrong with it and what does he see value in his method over it? What precisely is his method in contradistinction to the "Chassidic" method? The more detail and clarity, the better.

answers.text:
Fascinating question.

I preface this answer by openly stating this is not an area of expertise, but I was intrigued by the question and therefore did some digging...

So, firstly some background as to the Chassidish approach.

It writes here:

Chassidut is inwardly based upon the ancient doctrinal tradition of Kabbalah. Outwardly it gives new emphasis to the simple and joyful service of God, particularly through prayer and acts of loving-kindness. In Chassidic thought, the abstract and often impenetrable formulae of classical Kabbalah are recast into the psychological terms of human experience.

By using the individual’s own inner experience as an allegorical model for understanding the deepest mysteries of the universe, Chassidut both elevates the consciousness of the ordinary Jew as well as expands the conceptual territory of Kabbalistic thought. Indeed, the classical tradition of Kabbalah can be considered superficial relative to that of Chassidut. By focusing upon immediate experience, Chassidut identifies aspects of Divinity that the highly formal and abstract system of Kabbalistic induction leaves unexplored.

Another way of explaining the differing emphases of Kabbalah and Chassidut is to say that Kabbalah focuses on the "vessels" (kelim) of Creation while Chassidut deals with the "lights"(orot) that fill these vessels. This distinction is apparent even in the names attached to these two mystical traditions: The word Kabbalah in Hebrew is derived from the root kabal, "to serve as a receptacle or vessel," while the word Chassidut is constructed from the root chesed, "lovingkindness," an attribute often referred to symbolically as the light of day...

For more about detail about the specifics of the Chassidish approach to Kabbalah see here1. And also look at the 4th chapter of Mevo HaShearim by the Piaseczna Rebbe that deals exactly with this topic at length.

It would seem that this extra dimension, of "recasting" Kabbalah is what Chacham Hillel takes issue with.

I found this academic piece entitled The Boundaries of the Kabbalah: R. Yaakov Moshe Hillel and the Kabbalah in Jerusalem, Kabbalah and Contemporary Spiritual Revival, ed. Boaz Huss, Beer Sheva 2011, pp. 163-180 (English).

It is a good read and one of the things that it notes is how Chacham Hillel critiques the popularization of Kabbalah, warning against superficial interpretations and public display. As far as the chassidish approach, it is this 'deeper', discernment of the inner meaning of Kabbalah that he takes issue with. Or, in other words, whether the chassidish approach has both the capacity or right to explain it.

On page 69, footnote 42 it writes:

Since Lurianic Kabbalah rarely reveals the inner meaning (nimshal) of any one of its symbols (mashalim), it is a matter of controversy whether it is possible for anyone to discern it. The prevailing view among Sefardic Kabbalists (in Teiman, Iraq and North Africa) is that the nimshal is not available to us; we must simply learn Kabbalah as it has been revealed, as a sacred wisdom. As contemporary author Rabbi Ya’akov Moshe Hillel writes, summarizing the position of the leading Sefardic Kabbalist, Rabbi Shalom Sharabi (1720–1777): “There is no possibility whatsoever to grasp the inner ‘nimshal’ hidden in the text and its symbols. Ask yourself: Is it possible to interpret a riddle without first knowing the whole of the riddle itself, in all its detail? That is why our master Rabbi Shalom Sharabi—and following him, the works of most early and later Kabbalists—set their primary goal to study the teachings of Arizal, to know with as much clarity as possible, the stated symbolism (mashal hachitzon).... This is our primary task” [Rabbi Yaakov Moshe Hillel, Ahavas Shalom (Jerusalem, 2002), p. 124].

It also writes here in footnote 26 the following:

R. Yaakov Moshe Hillel writes about the conditions and methods for Zohar study in his Vayeshev HaYam, Part 3, Siman 32, sect. 11, which includes the following statement (the original Hebrew is followed by its translation and analysis):

… ובפרט יש להודיע ולהזהיר, לגבי אותם הקטעים שבזוהר העוסקים על דרך הסוד, שאיסור חמור הוא לתרגם אותם, כי אין בהם שייכות עם הפשט, והם סודות מופשטים ונעלמים, ורק שהלבישום במשלים גשמיים, אבל אין להם שום דמיון עם המשל החיצוני לפי האמת. ולכן אין בתרגומם שום תועלת כלל, כי הרי אין הדברים כפשטן כלל. ואדרבא הוא מזיק מאד, שמגשים בתכלית את הסודות. (ופשוט דגם ללשון הקודש אין נכון לתרגם לשונות כאלו). וכבר האריך בזה בתשובה רבינו הרי”ח טוב ז”ל בשו”ת רב פעלים (חלק א’ חלק יו”ד סימן נ”ו), וגזר חרם ושמתא על אדם אחד על שתרגם שיר השירים והאדרות וספר שומר אמונים ללשון ערבי המדוברת בין היהודים (באותיות עבריות). ואסר בכל תוקף לתרגם סודות התורה, עי”ש באורך.

“It should specifically be made known and the caution given, that there is a severe prohibition to translate those passages of the Zohar that relate to Kabbalistic secrets, as they do not have any associated literal meaning. They are abstracted and concealed secrets expressed using physical analogies. However, in truth, they are not comparable with the external analogy. Therefore, there is no purpose in translating them at all, as these matters are not like their literal meaning at all. On the contrary, it is very damaging, as it absolutely physicalizes the secret concepts. (It is obvious that it is also improper to translate these expressions [from Aramaic] into Hebrew.) This has already been elaborated upon by R. Yosef Chaim in a responsum in Rav Pe’alim (Part 1, Yoreh De’ah, Question 56). He decreed the excommunication of an individual who translated Shir Hashirim, the Idrot [Rabba and Zuta] and the work Shomer Emunim into Arabic that was spoken by the Jews (using Hebrew letters). He forbade, in the strongest terms, the translation of the secrets of the Torah. Refer there at length.”

So at least tentatively, we can suggest that he does not like the approach that Chassidish-based kabbalah takes where it probes and suggests meaning in the words of the Zohar and the like which, traditional sefardi mekubalim do not think anyone has license to do.

1 In short, Chassidish thought reinterprets Lurianic Kabbalah through the inner life of the human soul, rather than as a description of cosmic, metaphysical processes. Whereas classical Kabbalah, especially the Lurianic system, focused on the structure of the divine realms, the emanations (sefiros), and the dynamics of creation, contraction (tzimtzum), and repair (tikkun) in the supernal worlds, Chasidism internalised these doctrines, seeing them as psychological and spiritual processes within man.

questions.title_en: What is the discussion around the hashgacha behind our mesorah?
questions.question:
In the SeforimChatter podcast episode on Talmud Reclaimed, around minute 1:05:00, R' Shmuel Phillips mentions the idea that our mesorah is guided by hashgachah min hashomayim, and he quotes the Chazon Ish as saying such. In the next sentence he mentions other gedolim of the time who took a very different, more proactive approach of attempting to analyze kisvei yad, etc.

Can anyone detail this machlokes - the two positions and those who held them, as well as how they have played out in the century that has followed - i.e. how is this machlokes viewed in different camps nowadays? For example, I've heard that Briskers reject the shinuyei nuscha'os of the Rambam that Frankel produced.

answers.text:
Several scholars have discussed this topic in detail. For an excellent summary, I recommend Yaakov Spiegel's book עמודים בתולדות הספר העברי: הגהות ומגיהים (can be found in Otzar Hachochmah and Kotar). This volume, part of a series on the history of the Jewish book, is dedicated to examining sources from throughout Jewish history on the topic of hagahot (annotations) and manuscript variations. In chapter 15 he discussed views on the topic from the late Enlightenment period (end of the 18th century) and the early modern era (19-20th centuries). As he cited, several prior scholars have written regarding Chazon Ish's views regarding the role of manuscripts in the field of Torah study and halacha, including: Zvi A. Yehuda, 'Hazon Ish on Textual Criticism and Halakhah', Tradition 18 (1980), pp. 172-180; Rabbi Shnayer Z. Leiman, 'Hazon Ish on Textual Criticism and Halakhah - a Rejoinder', Tradition 19 (1981), pp. 301-310; Rabbi Moshe Bleich, 'The Role of Manuscripts in Halakhic Decision-Making: Hazon Ish, His Precursors and Contemporaries', Tradition 27 (1993), pp. 22-55, and more.

Zvi A. Yehuda began his discussion by stating that he was once asked by the eminent Orthodox scholar Rabbi Dr. Binyamin Menashe Levine to ask the Chazon Ish - whom Yehuda knew personally - why yeshiva students (and the yeshiva world at large) don't use his then-newly-published Otzar Ha'Geonim, a work he had toiled upon for years and which he believed would have greatly enriched the study of yeshiva students. According to Yehuda, Chazon Ish responded:

"The old material, we have; the new, we don't need. The sources already printed are found in the works of the Rishonim, organically within the context in which they are quoted and the way they are discussed and treated; the sources now printed for the first time from Geniza manuscripts, whatever their importance may be for academic study, are irrelevant for halakhic consideration."

In other words, usage of material - minute as it may be - that was not known to earlier generations, those whose works form the basis of the modern halachic corpus - is extremely problematic, as it is not contained within said corpus. As such, this material did not undergo generations of refinement within the rabbinic crucible and is therefore irrelevant for current discussions of halacha.

Elsewhere, Chazon Ish noted regarding the nusach of the Munich manuscript of the Talmud (Ms. Munich 95), which is the only manuscript we have today of the entire Bavli, and which formed the basis for Rabbi Refael Natan Neta Rabinovicz's Dikdukei Sofrim. In response to seeing its usage within halachic discussions, Chazon Ish wrote (קובץ אגרות מאת חזון איש, vol. 1, no. 33 [cited by Spiegel, p. 544]):

"...ולהגיה בגמ' עפ"י כת"י מינכן, וכי כל חכמי הדור מזמן הראשונים עד עכשיו כולם לא עמדו על האמת, מפני שסופר אחד טעה והוסיף דברים בגמ' מלבו, והכשיל את כל החכמים. ואני לא מהם ולא מהמונם, וכת"י שהיה ביד הראשונים מסרו נפשם עליהם, והשגחתו ית' שלא תשתכח תורה מישראל הגינה עליהם, וכשהחלו להדפיס את הגמ' מסרו חכמי הדור נפשם על זיקוקו והגהתו. ואם אמנם לפעמים נהנים מהכת"י לנקות השיבושים המתהוים בהמשך הזמן, אבל דבר שיצא מיד כל רבותנו בלי שום פקפוק - חלילה להרוס. הגע בעצמך, בשעה שיש שלשה כת"י לפנינו ושניהם שוין, אנו לוקחים את השנים ומניחים את האחד, ומאן לימא לאן דכת"י מינכן אינו מאותו שנתבטל ברוב בזמנו, ומאן לימא לן שלא היה ידוע לבעלי מדוקדק, ובכל אופן הוא בטל כחרס הנשבר נגד הגרסא המקובלת, וכי מני שהסופר טעה והשמיט איזה תיבות [...] נבנה מגדלים, ואולי כן שהסופר השמיטם ולא מיד חכמים הוא, אבל כשאנו סומכים על הקבלה, תורת רש"י ותוספות וכל החכמים, ודאי היא התורה, וכמעט שלא ראיתי תועלת להגיע אל האמת ע"י הגירסאות שמחפשים מהגניזות, רק כולם תועלת לעוות משפט ולעקם את האמת, וראוי היה לגונזם, שההפסד יתר על השכר."

"...And to make corrections in the talmud according to Ms. Munich, and [should we think] that all of the sages of past generations did not uncover the truth, all because one scribe made a mistake and added things to the gemara from his mind, and caused all of the sages to stumble. And I am not of them and their kind, and manuscripts that were in the hands of the Rishonim they gave their lives over them, and the Blessed One's providence that the Torah shall not be forgotten from Yisrael protected them, and when the gemara began to be printed, the sages of the generation gave their lives to purifying and correcting it (=the nusach). And even though sometimes we enjoy from fixing errors formed over time within manuscripts, but something that undoubtedly came from the hands of our rabbis - God forbid that we destroy. See for yourself, when we have three manuscripts before us and two are equal, we take the two and leave the third, and who told you that Ms. Munich was not one of those that was canceled out in time, and how do you know that it (Ms. Munich) was not known to the annotating sages, and in any case, it (Ms. Munich) is canceled out like a broken pottery sherd in the face of the accepted (widespread) version, should we build towers from a version where the scribe made a mistake and left out some words, and perhaps the scribe is the one who left out the words and not sages, but when we rely on tradition, the Torah of Rashi and Tosfot and all of the sages, it is certainly the Torah, and I hardly saw any usage for reaching the truth based on versions pulled out from genizot, their entire usage is to simply distort the law and bend the truth, and it is appropriate to bury them, for the loss is greater than the gain."

In short, according to the Chazon Ish, widespread versions of sources are more trustworthy than ancient manuscripts, because we must believe that the popular versions were ones that were checked out, properly corrected and purified by earlier sages, and that Hashem's providence led to our possession of these popular versions. Chazon Ish also produced arguments specifically against Ms. Munich: It may well be that this manuscript was already known at the time of its production to be of poor quality in terms of its content. In the end, we really do not know what Jews of the past thought of its nusach. In other words, old and complete isn't necessarily better.

That's not to say that the Chazon Ish would have been entirely against the usage of manuscripts, as he himself noted that sometimes scribal errors may creep into manuscript traditions that had passed under the hands of sages. Rabbi Bleich in his article (pp. 38-39) noted a case where Rabbi Wosner ruled in favor of a version of Ra'avad cited by the Rosh and the Shulchan Aruch against the Chatam Sofer's interpretation of the Ra'avad, as a version of Ra'avad based on newly-discovered manuscripts proved that the former poskim's versions were more accurate than Chatam Sofer's, thereby rendering the latter's interpretation irrelevant. Such a case conforms with the Chazon Ish's view, according to Rabbi Bleich.

Rabbi Moshe Feinstein agreed with the Chazon Ish's position to some extent. His main criticism of critical editions of Jewish works was that they were often produced by academics and not men truly learned in Torah, which would often lead to severe mistakes in their reasoning. See a summary of his view in Rabbi Bleich's article, pp. 37-38. Rabbi Shlomo Zevin, who was part of the team that worked on Dikdukei Sofrim Ha'Shalem, agreed that manuscripts may only be used if they are in agreement with a textual tradition that can be found among the Rishonim. His rationale was that we today do not have the ability to discern correct textual versions and must trust the judgement of the giants of previous generations (Dikdukei Sofrim Ha'Shalem, vol. 5: Ketubot, pt. 1, p. 12; mentioned also by Rabbi Bleich, p. 42).

But the Chazon Ish also had some opponents on the issue. Rabbi Yechiel Yaakov Weinberg (author of Shu"t Seridei Esh), for example, noted on one hand that there is no reason to assume that a unique textual tradition found in the work of a rishon was necessarily flawed. The reverse may be true: That that book preserves the true, correct version. Therefore, Rabbi Weinberg wholeheartedly supported the publication of critical editions. See a summary of his view in Rabbi Bleich's article, pp. 35-37.

Another of the Chazon Ish's opponents on the matter was Rabbi Menachem Mendel Kasher (most well-know for his Torah Shelemah compendium), who began publishing the Gemara Shelemah, a critical edition of the Talmud based on multiple manuscripts. On the occasion of the publication of two volumes from a separate project, Yad Ha'Rav Herzog's Mishna Zeraim and Masechet Ketubot of Mif'al Ha'Shas Ha'Shalem, Rabbi Kasher published an essay on the importance of using manuscripts in the study of gemara ("להופעת שני כרכים ממפעל הש"ס השלם", Noam 16 [5733/1973], § Halachah, pp. 165-182). This essay was prefaced by an essay written by Rabbi Yisrael Rosen on the importance of Rabbi Kasher's work in the field of talmudic manuscripts ("להופעת שני כרכים ממפעל הש"ס השלם", ibid., pp. 156-165), and included copies of letters Rabbi Weinberg sent Rabbi Kasher (and herein we see the differences between the Chazon Ish and Rabbi Weingarten). Among other things, Rabbi Kasher responded to the Chazon Ish (simply referring to him as a "gadol ha'dor" without explicitly stating who he was speaking about. However, he quotes the above passage from Igrot, vol. 1):

Rabbi Kasher opened by expressing surprise at the Chazon Ish's wholesale rejection of manuscripts simply due to one scribal error in Ms. Munich, which led another contemporaneous rabbi to reach a faulty conclusion regarding that specific passage. He then noted the importance of Ms. Munich:

  • It is the only complete Shas manuscript that has survived to this day.
  • It was used by the author of the Korban Netanel.
  • Several prominent rabbis welcomed Rabbi Rabinovicz's publication of Dikdukei Sofrim, based on Ms. Munich. Rabbi Yosef Natansohn (author of Shoel U'Meshiv) in particular greatly valued the book and heaped praises on it. Other gedolim who praised the publication include Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan Spektor, Rabbi Yaakov Ettlinger, and Rabbi Shlomo Kluger.

Rabbi Kasher then noted the flaws in the Chazon Ish's arguments:

  • The process of preserving two manuscripts against a third is only relevant for Written Torah (Tanach). The poskim never argued that the same rule applied to manuscript variants of Oral Torah works.
  • The reverse is actually true: There were poskim who argued that a manuscript with a unique textual tradition must also be taken into account (חוששין לו).
  • Many gedolim over the ages used variant manuscripts and textual traditions as a basis for their arguments.
  • The claim that "when the gemara began to be printed, the sages of the generation gave their lives to purifying and correcting it (=the nusach)" is simply incorrect - studies of the history of the printing of the Talmud shows that no gedolim were involved in correcting the nusach of the printed Shas. Again, the reverse is true - when gedolim began studying printed gemaras, they marked down the vast number of mistakes found in these editions.

It is therefore evident, noted Rabbi Kasher, that the many mistakes in the printed editions necessitate a critical study of the textual tradition of the Talmud, to discern what is the most correct text. Rabbi Kasher finished off this section of the essay by noting that the same (regarding using manuscripts and variant textual traditions to discern the correct text) should be argued regarding other Jewish works, from the time of the Geonim and onwards.

Where we are today: Rabbi Kasher had opened his essay by noting that it's clear to him that not every person has the intellectual capability to sift through textual variations and to properly understand how each variation arose, but he hoped that other talmidei chachamim (Yechidei Segulah as he referred to them) will join him, perhaps via Yad Ha'Rav Herzog, in working on producing a critical edition of the Shas and other important Jewish works, and that these editions will be welcomed by the yeshiva world. Nowadays, however, to my knowledge, it seems that for the general gemara (and other works)-studying public, the old printed editions largely remain triumphant, while the study of manuscript variants is mainly limited to the halls of academia, though can also be found among some individuals in the Torah/yeshiva world. Some yeshivas and Torah-background-type institutes publish on occasion new critical editions of Jewish books, typically the result of a joint effort between members of the institutions and more academically-leaning scholars. Sometimes such editions merit general popularity and sometimes they remain obscure.1 It's not entirely clear to me whether there are prominent "camps" today as there were back then (last century). Perhaps someone else can shed light on the matter.

1 Anecdotally, there's such an institute that's connected to my yeshiva (it was essentially founded by alumni and is situated near the yeshiva; note that I am otherwise unaffiliated with this institute) that published, among other books, a new edition of the S'fat Emet. I've heard that the Gerrer Rebbe keeps this edition on his desk.

questions.title_en: Does Piggul intention need to be expressed verbally or merely mentally?
questions.question: The intention to do one of the avodahs outside the correct time is called piggul. Does the intention need to be expressed verbally or merely mentally?

answers.text: Rashi and Tosafos say it must be verbal. Rambam and Sefer Hachinuch says mental intent is enough. See Artscoll Zevachim 27b note 28 and Menachos 2b end of note 25 for further sources that discuss the matter.

questions.title_en: Are there "Godparents" in Judaism? What should an honorary Jewish "Godparent" know about traditions, celebrations, and gifts?
questions.question:
I'm from a Christian background and have been asked to be an "honorary Godmother" in a Jewish context. I'm trying to understand what that role means, if anything, within Jewish tradition.

In Catholicism, Godparents typically have a formal role in religious milestones such as Baptism, First Communion, and Confirmation, and they often give symbolic gifts (e.g., rosary beads, prayer books, Bibles).

My questions:

Is there an equivalent to "Godparents" in Judaism, either officially or informally?

If someone is considered an "honorary Godparent" in a Jewish family, are there traditions, customs, or expectations they should be aware of?

Are there specific Jewish lifecycle events (e.g., baby naming, Bar/Bat Mitzvah, etc.) where an honorary Godparent would typically be involved or invited?

What are some meaningful, appropriate gifts one might give for Jewish milestones (comparable to religious gifts in Catholicism)?

I'm eager to learn and do right by this role, even if it's symbolic. Any insight into how this might vary across denominations (Reform, Conservative, Orthodox) would also be helpful.

answers.text: While not truly an "equivalent," the sandak who holds the baby boy at his brit milah is by some considered to have a role like that of a "godparent."

questions.title_en: Praying for a specific job
questions.question:
The Gemara in Moed Kattan brings the story of how we shouldn’t pray for a specific shidduch because if that girl is “the one” then Hashem will give her to us, but if she isn’t then you are messing yourself up.

The Gemara speaks about praying for something specific only in regard to shidduchim, but what about in other areas? Can I pray for a specific job role, or must I pray in general for parnassah and leave it up to Hashem?

The same can really apply to any area in life.

questions.title_en: Zera Yisrael 50% jewish is patrilineal Jewish,?
questions.question: I am a Soler Mater es Quadam 50 % Jewish and not raised jewish, is there a way to be Jewish then my biological father is American Jewish whom i dont know he was a Vietnam veteran. I even have dreams of shechita, it is hard to understand i have a non Jewish mother and non Jewish father. A childhood dentist told me once i am a descendant of the hebrew.

answers.text:
"Zera Yisrael", is a term that rings with a Jewish flavor. Nevertheless, Jewish religious law articulates quite clearly, that a child who is born to a Jewish father and a non-Jewish mother is considered to be a non-Jew.

If they sincerely want to convert to Judaism, they are welcomed, and they need to go the full conversion process. This includes exhibiting a serious level of commitment to religious observance, which is a prerequisite for conversion. Those of so-called “Zera Yisrael” are not granted any “shortcuts” due to their genealogical affiliation. After successfully completing the process, they will be considered “Jews by choice”, not by birth.

questions.question: Can you steal something with the intent of paying back something more valuable than the item that you stole?

questions.title_en: Connection between steps of Beis HaMikdash, Shir Hamaalos, and Mabul above mountains
questions.question:
There are 15 Shir Hamaalos in Tehillim (120–134), 15 steps in the Beis Hamikdash where the Levi'im sang, and 15 amos of water above the highest mountains by the Mabul. What is the connection?

(There are many more 15s, but I'll limit for now.)

answers.text: So look, the steps of the Beis HaMikdash - specifically these fifteen ma'alos that go up from the Ezras Nashim to the Ezras Yisrael - they have a very deep connection, mamash, to the fifteen "Shir HaMa'alos" in Tehillim, you know what I mean? These pesukim, the Levi'im were singing them on these very steps, and it represents, like, an aliyah - an ascent - in ruchniyus and kedushah. And the number fifteen itself, chamesh-esrei, is very significant, ken? Because it's connected to Hashem's Name - yud-hei (י-ה) - which shows us there's a kesher, a connection, between the physical aliyah and the Shechina, the divine presence, davka. Now, regarding the Mabul, the flood - the Torah tells us explicitly that the water rose fifteen amos above the highest mountains, right there in Bereishis 7:20. This number could symbolize, in a symbolic way, the koach of HaKadosh Baruch Hu that encompasses everything - both in destruction and also in protection of the briyah, the creation. So mamash, the number fifteen in these contexts - it connects the whole inyan of aliyah, of divine presence, and of Hashem's all-encompassing power, you see?

questions.title_en: Restrictions on Cohanim who are duchening
questions.question:
During "duchening," when the cohanim give the Bircat Cohanim, they start with a bracha:

בְּרוּךְ אַתָּה יְ' אֱ' מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם, אֲשֶׁר קַדְּשָׁנוּ בַּקְדְשָׁתוֹ שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן וְצַיֵּנוּ לְבָרֵךְ אֶת עַמּוֹ יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּאַהֲבָה.

... bless his people Israel with love.

Questions

  1. What are the Mishnah/Gemerah (or later) sources that discuss this bracha?
  2. Especially: are there sources that discuss the required (or disallowed) mindset of a Cohen to enable or disable him from making this bracha and performing the Bircat Cohanim ceremony?

Is it true that if the Cohen isn't in the mindset to bless the congregation "with love" then that's an issue for him?

questions.title_en: Correct wording in Lecha Dodi / "Gam (BeSimcha) BeRina..."
questions.question:
In the Sephardic version of Lecha Dodi, we say: "גם בשמחה, ברינה ובצהלה".

The Ashkenazic version is "גם ברינה ובצהלה", which seems more correct to me: The stanza is already quite long, and it doesn’t feel likely that there’s yet another word.

Do we know what the original wording was? And when or why it may have changed?

questions.title_en: Adding a line of Tanya before kaddish
questions.question:
It is common in Chabad after davening for someone to say a Mishna from Mikvaos 7, followed by Makkos 3:15, followed by mourners saying Kaddish. I observed a Chabad rabbi doing this, but he mumbled something between the mishna and saying kaddish. He told me later it was a line from Tanya but didn't elaborate.

Does anyone know what this was? How common is this practice?

answers.text:
Very common. It is a minhag that the Lubavitcher Rebbe was observed doing and the verse is the first one from chapter two of tanya.

וְנֶפֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִית בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, הִיא חֵלֶק אֱלוֹהַּ מִמַּעַל מַמָּשׁ

And the second Jewish soul is literally a part of Gd above.

For more elaboration on the meaning, see Lessons in Tanya which can be found for free at chabad.org or purchased from a variety of seforim stores. Another great resource for understanding Tanya is Rabbi Yossi Paltiel's website insidechassidus.org.

questions.title_en: English-language sefer Orach Chaim tidbits

questions.title_he: Is this pronunciation of ה acceptable?
questions.question:
I have a friend who’s often the ש״ץ of a casual Minyan.

I’ve noticed that he occasionally pronounces ה very emphatically, such that it becomes strongly pharyngealized, and thus identical to the Mizrahi pronunciation of ח (henceforth “ħ”). He does this apparently at random.

It’s known that one should be careful not to mix up certain letters, since doing so can radically alter the meaning of certain words. One example found in the Talmud is accidentally pronouncing a ה like ח, regarding the roots ה־ל־ל and ח־ל־ל. The former means “praise”, while the latter means “desecrate”; so it’s important to pronounce the ה correctly in words derived from ה־ל־ל.

If my friend normally pronounced ח as “ħ”, this would obviously be problematic. Thing is, he pronounces ח the same way as כ, like Ashkenazim.

Is “ħ” considered a pronunciation of ח for my friend, even though that he doesn’t use it for ח? In other words, does “ħ” have an objective status as a pronunciation of ח?
(Does “ħ” being the original pronunciation make a difference? What about the fact that a portion of the minyan does use “ħ” for ח?)

If not, is “ħ” considered a valid free allophone of ה for my friend? Or is it still halachically undesirable for whatever reason?

In short, should he be more careful how he pronounces ה?

questions.title_en: Does Earth having a second moon affect halacha?
questions.question: Apparently according to NASA Earth currently has a second moon, until the year 2083. I never considered the possibility that the Earth could gain additional moons. Whether or not the current asteroid is halachically classified as a moon, I would like to know if in the event that the Earth were to gain a natural satellite that would be halachically defined as a moon, would this impact Judaism in any way?

answers.text:
The "moon" is actually misnamed as such, and much of the media around it is a bit overhyped. The new asteroid is not orbiting Earth, but conducting an orbit around the sun that is close to Earth's. As such, it is not a "moon" but a space rock that happens to be close to us, and will dissapear in 2083 because it is not in a stable orbit around Earth.

Also, like @RabbiKaii and @shmosel said, halachically "moon" refers to Earth's current moon, the rounded object you can see in the sky.

If halachically a "moon" were any object orbiting the earth that you could see, than we could celebrate Rosh Chodesh every 90 minutes because the ISS could be considered a moon.

If earth really did have a second moon that was astronomically defined as one, I still think that halachically only our moon that we already are familiar with would count for calendar purposes.

As for the premise of the question, I think it is valid, since technically the question actually also includes the question inside a question of "what is halachically defined as a moon?"

questions.title_en: Abarbanel's Timeline of Shoftim and Shmuel

Does anyone have any resources on Abarbanel's timeline in Shmuel 1 Ch. 13?

Anything would help tremendously.

My real question: After Abarbanel states his opinion of the timeline, he states two results that pertain to that chapter. In the first one, he states that Shmuel was judge from Eli's death to Shaul's Coronation [20 years], adding that that includes the 20 years that the Aron was in Kiryas Yearim before Klal Yisroel did Teshuva, and then 5 or 6 years before Shaul's coronation. That would mean that from Eli's death to Shaul's coronation is 25-26 years, not 20 as he mentioned in the timeline! Any thoughts?

answers.text: Here's a timeline I made (click on the picture to enlarge it; the spaces between points on the timeline are a rough estimate and not intended to be accurate). The Abarbanel preferred including Shamgar's reign within the 80 years between Ehud and Yavin, but noted a variant option for Shamgar, having him rule for one year. This would shift all dates forward by one year until Shmuel's time, and then cutting down Shmuel's reign as judge by one year (19 years total instead of 20). Abarbanel assumed that all dates were accurate except for the "300 years" that had passed since the Israelite conquest of the Amorite (ex-Ammonite) territory in the 40th year from the Exodus, stated by Yiftach in his speech to the king of Ammon. questions.title_en: Why did six souls inherit specific marks from Adam?
questions.question:
Shalom,

The Zohar describes six souls who inherited specific traits from Adam. They are: Samson, Saul, Asael, Absalom, Zedekiah and Josiah. They inherited strength, neck, speed, hair, eyes and nostrils. Sadly they seemed unable to handle it, for they all died by the means of their specific trait.

It is written in the Zohar about this:

Chayei Sarah: Verse 42

Rabbi Yehuda said that when the Holy One, blessed be He, first created Adam-while he still was unformformed flesh and had no soul He said to the angel who was assigned over the images of men, "Look, and form in this form six men, SAMSON, SAUL, ASAEL, JOSIAH, ZEDEKIAH, AND ABSHALOM. This is the meaning of the verse, "And begot a son in his own likeness, after his image and called his name Seth" (Beresheet 5:3). The Aramaic word Seth means six AND REFERS TO THE SIX PEOPLE MENTIONED.

Where can I find more information about this subject? Why did God chose to make it like this that those six are similar to Adam?

questions.title_en: If you are supposed to pray towards Eretz Yisrael, why do many American synagogues only face east?

I did a bit of computer programming with Google Earth and a straight great circle line from, say, Los Angeles to Jerusalem is actually north-northeast, and actually going straight east (not due east, which is not a straight line) would land you in roughly South Africa.

Does halakha involve pointing "towards Jerusalem" as a straight great circle line or simply pointing east (and north or south, depending on your latitude)?

Another question by Shaul Behr asked why Manhattan pointed south south west, and this seems like it would actually be the correct direction, since a straight line in that direction would actually hit Israel!

My guess is a ruling on this would be relatively recent since up until ~1400 CE people thought the earth was flat, which would eliminate this problem, and also most of the diaspora communities still lived relatively near Israel to the point where this kind of calculation is not as counterintuitive.

questions.title_en: What is the Chabad tradition for starting the day as a Jew alone in the morning?
questions.question:
I understand Chabad as having a unique style of Chassidism, emphasizing an awareness of the mystical aspects of Jewish practices while following Jewish tradition with orthodox rigor and zeal. I am not an orthodox Jew and don't know how the day usually starts for followers of the Chabad traditions. When I try to look it up, I mostly find prayers that are meant to be said during a service with a minyan.

How do Jews following Chabad start their days when they're alone and not able to go to a morning service? What are the rituals and prayers said?

More broadly I'd love to learn this answer for the whole day, how one structures their day, but even just understanding morning routines would be helpful. For example, I know the Modeh Ani prayer is said when one first opens their eyes in the morning, and then comes washing one's hands. Then at some point, laying tefillin facing east and saying some prayers. But I am missing lots of details and clarity, especially on what prayers are said when alone vs. in a communal service.

answers.text:
1. The Modeh Ani (see source for the positioning).
  2. Washing Negel Vaaser.
  3. Dressing, going to a Mikva (ritual bath) if there's one in the area (some may even use a pool).
  4. Morning Prayers, Shema.
  5. Mezonot (pastries), coffee / tea to taste.
  6. Learn Chabad Chassidus.
  7. Shacharis. Whether or not you're praying with a minyan, preparing for prayer is the same: Start at Hareinu Mekabel, until Eizehu Mekomon at this point we lay the Talit (if applicable) and Teffilin. Recite Eizehu Mekoimon. After the Yehi Ratzon if you were praying with a minyan, the Chazzan would say Kaddish Derabbanan. Continue on to Hodu through Yishtabach. By a minyan, the Chazan would say Half Kaddish. Continue on to Yoitzer Or through after the Amida. By a minyan, at this point, the chazan would recite the repetition of the Amida. Continue on to Viduy (if applicable), through Oleinu (there are three Kaddeshim a Chazzan would do in between, and on Monday and Thursday there's the Torah reading). After the conclusion of prayer (Al Tirah), we say the Rebbe's Kapital (Psalms Chapter 124), and the Rebbitzins (125). Then Psalms Chapter 20, your own Chapter (the year of age you're entering, e.g. if you turned 30, you entered your 31st year - Chapter 31). Then the Daily Tehillim. After which, a Chazzan who is mourning would say Mourner's Kaddish. We remove our Rashi Teffilin and lay Rabbeinu Tam and (Shema, Vehaya etc). Then the Seven Remembrances.
  8. Study the Chitas and Rambam. This is done at a certain point during the day; many do this in the morning.

Mincha and Mariv follow; many set a time to learn a portion of Nigla at a certain point.

There are thousands of Chabad Chassidim away from the regular community element, hundreds not even having a Minyan to attend. That is because they are Shluchim, emissaries of the Rebbe, spreading Judaism in the most central regions to the far flung areas.

Praying, in our general view, isn't just a time we request our personal physical-spiritual needs from G-d, rather a format of connection to Him. It's not magical, though. To get there we learn about Him (learning Chabad Chassidus before praying), and contemplate about Him (using what we learned). To enhance the spirituality, we make our physicality most able - by eating some sort of Pastry, hence nourishing our bodies to be nourished by our soul.

With that foundation laid, the day is set on its proper path: renewal of energy and commitment to the service of G-d.

questions.title_en: Source that Adam Harishon drank 926 *luggim* of wine
questions.question:
I heard that Adam Harishon drank 926 luggim of wine from the etz hadaat (according to R' Yehuda's opinion in Berachot 40a that it bore grapes).

This seems plausible according to the tradition that Adam Harishon was physically gigantic (see haggigah 12), and since David Hamelech does tikkun for Adam (as he received his 70 years from Adam's 1,000 - see Zohar Lech-lecha 31).

David Hamelech lived 57 years from bar mitzvah to death. If you count a revi'it of wine for Friday night kiddush, that is 4 revi'its/month = 1 log/month.

Add in 21 Adar Shenis, and David drank 705 lug in all his adult Friday nights.

Remaining for tikkun is 221 luggim, which is why yoma 76 says the cup David will bless at seudat livyatan (see pesahim 119) will be 221 = gematria of "revaya" from Tehilim (kosi revaya)

I heard this in the name of a midrash, and also in the name of meir enei hachamim, but can't find any source that Adam drank exactly 926 luggim. Where is that source?

questions.title_en: Why are there two different versions of the vowels in lekh-lekha?
questions.question:
Preparing to leyn next week, I noticed that a word in Bereshit 12:3 appears very slightly differently in different versions. On the version on Sefaria (JPS's Contemporary Torah) and tikkun.io, it's מְבָ֣רְכֶ֔יךָ , while in my the weekday readings section of my Artscroll and my Koren, as well as Chabad's version, it's מְבָ֣רֲכֶ֔יךָ . In particular, under the resh, there's a shva (na) in the former and a khataf patakh in the latter.

The difference in pronunciation is minor in my pronunciation, but I'd like to leyn the "right" pronunciation. I'd also like to understand what's going on. Is this a typo in one? Are there multiple versions of the Masoretic text? Do different groups use different versions? Is there a list of variations somewhere so I know when to be aware of this?

answers.text:
See the comments and answers at DoubleAA’s link.

In the Masoretic era, Shva was pronounced exactly like chataf-Patach by default. So many Masoretes would replace certain instances of Shva naʿ with a chataf-Patach, in order to clarify that the Shva should be pronounced in that situation.

Nowadays, most Jews pronounce Shva naʿ like Segol, so the Masoretic trick to disambiguate Shva naʿ doesn’t apply to us. (The modern equivalent is printing Shva naʿ in a bold font.)

Several modern tiḳḳūnīm have unfortunately failed to understand this, and attempt to “fix” the vocalization of the Chumash by replacing Shva with chataf-Patach and claiming the vowel should be pronounced as such, as opposed to Shva naʿ. This is historically mistaken. In all such words, the essential vowel is a simple Shva naʿ. That’s the vowel that was intended by the Masoretes, and that’s the vowel we’re meant to pronounce.

In short, the Shva’s right.

I will not address the pronunciation part of the question, which has already been ably addressed above. But will address this part of the question:

Are there multiple versions of the Masoretic text? Do different groups use different versions? Is there a list of variations somewhere so I know when to be aware of this?

Edit: the answer I originally gave (preserved below) is for the wrong word. The correct word, i.e. the word asked about in the original question, does not have חטף פתח on its ר in the authoritative manuscripts, but does have חטף פתח on its ר in the printed tradition, stemming back, as it often does, to the 2nd Venice MG (see comment below).

==== original, flawed answer appears below ====

MAM's decision was to have simple shewa, where that shewa is supplemented by varika in some editions. (MAM restricts the use of חטף shewa to gutturals but if one or more manuscripts of interest use חטף shewa on a non-guttural, it notes this with a varika.) To understand MAM's decision, and to see where notable manuscripts "land" on this issue, see an edition of MAM that shows its documentation, such as "MAM with doc."

Just to have it right here, here is how the documentation currently reads:

וַאֲבָֽרְﬞכָה֙ =ו,ל1,ש,ש1 וכמו כן בתיגאן ובדפוסים

ל,ק3?=וַאֲבָֽרֲכָה֙ (חטף); בכתי"ק3 נראה שיד שניה הוסיפה קו של פתח בחלל של האות.

הערת ברויאר

For a definition of the terse abbreviations ("sigils") like ו and ל1 used above to identify manuscripts, see MAM's documentation of its sources for the Torah.

questions.title_en: Where in Tanach do we find a jewel as a source of light
questions.question: I am trying to find where in Tanach, other than in Noah's ark, is there a jewel as a source of light. I have checked the chumash in reference to light from the basket Moses was placed in and I believe there might have been some kind of jewel as light in the fish that swallowed Jonah.

answers.text:
As per @DoubleAA's comment above, I don't know if you are specifically after sources direct in Tanach or also the commentaries, but if the latter, there is an incredibly insightful piece from Rabbeinu Bachya when detailing the choshen (in Parshas Teruma 28:15) and the various precious stones that were used.

When describing the stone that was used for Shevet Levi, it writes:

לוי היה מפותח על ברקת והוא הקרבונקל"א נקראת ברקת על שם שנוצצת כברק ומאירה כנר וכן תרגום ברקן, והוא אבן שתלה נח בתיבה ממה שכתוב (בראשית ו׳:ט״ז) צהר תעשה לתיבה והנביא קראה אקדח שנאמר (ישעיהו נ״ד:י״ב) ושעריך לאבני אקדח על שם שקודח כגחלת והוא מלשון (שם נ) קודחי אש, ונתנה ללוי מפני ששבט לוי היו מאירין בתורה כענין שנאמר (דברים ל״ג:י׳) יורו משפטיך ליעקב ותורתך לישראל, וכן משה שהיה משבט לוי כשנולד נתמלא כל הבית אורה ונאמר בו כי קרן עור פניו וכתיב (קהלת ח׳:א׳) חכמת אדם תאיר פניו, וסגולת האבן הזאת שהיא מחכימת פתי ומאירת העינים מלבד שמשתמשין בעצם גופה כמו שמשתמשין באור הנר...

The stone which bore the name of Levi was the ברקת, known popularly as carbuncle (a rounded gemstone without facets). It is so called as it flashes just like a bolt of lightning, ברק. It illuminates like a lamp. Onkelos also translates it as ברקן, a flashing stone. This was the gemstone Noach hung in the ark to provide him with light. The Torah referred to this light in Genesis 6,15 צהר תעשה לתבה. Isaiah refers to it as אקדח, in Isaiah 54,12 where, speaking of the future of Israel he writes: ”I will make your battlements rubies and your gates of precious stones, i.e. לאבני אקדח.” The name is justified as it appears glowing like red-hot coals. A similar expression occurs also in Isaiah 50,11: “kindlers of fire.” The reason this stone was chosen to symbolise Levi was that the Levites illuminate the people by teaching them spiritual illumination, i.e. Torah, as we know from Deut. 33,10 יורו משפטיך ליעקב ותורתך לישראל, “they teach Your judgments to Yaakov and Your Torah to Israel.” We also know of Moses, who was of the tribe of Levi, that the whole house was filled with light when he was born as the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah 1,24) interpreted the words in Exodus there (Exodus 2,2) that “she (his mother) saw that he was good.” Furthermore, when Moses returned from Mount Sinai with the second sets of Tablets the Torah testified that the skin of his face emitted rays of light (Exodus 34,29). We have another verse (Kohelet 8,1) “a man’s wisdom lights up his face.” The positive value of this gemstone is that it is apt to enlighten the foolish, providing him with insights he never had. This is in addition to the general usefulness of that jewel in providing light just as does a lamp.

questions.title_en: What's the source of this story about pronouncing letters in the Talmud?
questions.question:
I remember reading a story in the Talmud about a Rabbi, who was seemingly being made fun of for his voice by another Rabbi. Someone else, maybe his father, told him to reply that the second person was constantly saying heresy whenever he prayed, because he pronounced Chet like Heh. (I think this referred to the root ch-l-l ("profane"), which he pronounced like h-l-l ("praise"), which reversed the meaning of whatever verse was under discussion.)

Where in the Talmud is this story found?

(Note: AI was used to make sure this was grammatical and clear)

answers.text:
It’s in Megillah 24b

אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי חִיָּיא לְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בַּר רַבִּי: אִלְמָלֵי אַתָּה לֵוִי — פָּסוּל אַתָּה מִן הַדּוּכָן, מִשּׁוּם דַּעֲבֵי קָלָךְ. אֲתָא אֲמַר לֵיהּ לַאֲבוּהּ. אֲמַר לֵיהּ: זִיל אֵימָא לֵיהּ: כְּשֶׁאַתָּה מַגִּיעַ אֵצֶל ״וְחִכִּיתִי לַה׳״, לֹא נִמְצֵאת מְחָרֵף וּמְגַדֵּף?

The Gemara relates that Rabbi Ḥiyya once said to Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: If you were a Levite, you would be disqualified from singing on the platform in the Temple courtyard because your voice is thick. Rabbi Shimon went and told his father, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, what Rabbi Ḥiyya had said. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said to him: Go and say to him: When you study and reach the verse: “And I will wait upon [veḥikkiti] the Lord” (Isaiah 8:17), will you not be a maligner and a blasphemer? Rabbi Ḥiyya, who was from Babylonia, was unable to differentiate between the letters ḥet and heh, and he would therefore pronounce the word veḥikkiti as vehikkiti, which means: And I will strike.

questions.title_en: Origins of the Perizi
questions.question:
Do we know the origins of the people known as the Perizi people who are mentioned in Parashath Lech Lecha, Sefer Bereishith 13:7?
Who was their ancestor going back towards Noach?

answers.text: Ibn Ezra (Shemos 3:8) says that they are from צידון, the son of כנען (see Bereishis 10:15).

Following Ibn Ezra's suggestion as brought in @S. Dixler's answer, various supercommentaries on Ibn Ezra attempted to explain the rationale behind the identification. The best explanation I've seen was brought in Rabbi Yitzchak Meller's Ezra Le'Havin on Shemot 3:8:

"צידון. שהרי מצינו גבי אברהם והכנעני והפריזי אז וגו' הרי שהוציא את הפריזי לחשבו לבד. לז"א (=לפיכך זאת אומרת) שהפריזי הוא צידון בכור כנען. שהיה גבולו לבד מהכנעני כמ"ש (=כמו שכתוב) ויהי גבול הכנעני מצידון. ונקרא הפריזי כמ"ש בשופטים אל עם שוקט ובוטח כמשפט צידונים. משמע שהיו יושבים בערי הפרזות."

"Tzidon. For we find regarding Avraham "and the Canaanite and the Perizzite were at the time etc", for we find that the Perizzites were viewed as separate. Therefore, that means that the Perizzite is Tzidon, Canaan's eldest. For his territory 's boundaries were separate from that of the Canaanite, as it is written: "The Canaanite territory extended from Tzidon". And they were called Perizzite, as it is written in Shoftim "to...a tranquil and unsuspecting people", "after the manner of the Tzidonim". Meaning, that they lived in unwalled cities.

In other words, the suggested rationale behind the Ibn Ezra's statement is thus: During the time of Avraham, the Perizzites were apparently a prominent enough people to be described as separate from the rest of the Canaanites. Elsewhere, in the description of the Canaanite families in Parashat Noach, Tzidon (Sidon) is also described as distinct from the other families, as all of the families were included in the territory of Canaan, while Tzidon was described as having a separate territory. As for why the Tzidonim were known as Perizzites, this question is clarified in a verse in Shoftim which describes people from Tzidon (or at least closely connected to them) living tranquil lives, which appears to indicate they lived in unwalled cities - not fearing any enemy attacks.

From the hebrew wiki entry on פריזי

The Perizzite are never mentioned anywhere separately from the other Canaanite nations. In fact, they aren't t even mentioned in the list of the sons of Canaan:

"וּכְנַעַן, יָלַד אֶת-צִידֹן בְּכֹרוֹ וְאֶת-חֵת: וְאֶת-הַיְבוּסִי, וְאֶת-הָאֱמֹרִי, וְאֵת הַגִּרְגָּשִׁי:" — Book of Genesis, Chapter 10, verses 15–16

Arel Segal Halevi writes that it is possible that the term “Perizzite” is merely a designation given to a portion of Canaan’s descendants (perhaps among the sons of Canaan who did not become separate nations — such as the Arkite, the Sinite, the Arvadite, etc.), possibly because they lived in villages and unwalled towns (arei perazot), as it is written:

"וְעַכְבְּרֵי הַזָּהָב מִסְפַּר כָּל עָרֵי פְלִשְׁתִּים לַחֲמֵשֶׁת הַסְּרָנִים מֵעִיר מִבְצָר וְעַד כֹּפֶר הַפְּרָזִי..." (Book of Samuel I, Chapter 6, verse 18). And Rashi explains: "כפר הפרזי" — a village without a wall.

Also written in Ezekiel: "וְאָמַרְתָּ אֶעֱלֶה עַל אֶרֶץ פְּרָזוֹת אָבוֹא הַשֹּׁקְטִים יֹשְׁבֵי לָבֶטַח כֻּלָּם יֹשְׁבִים בְּאֵין חוֹמָה וּבְרִיחַ וּדְלָתַיִם אֵין לָהֶם" (Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 38, verse 11).

It may be inferred that peoples who lived in unwalled towns were peaceful nations engaged in trade rather than war. Accordingly, the Perizzite was also a quiet and tranquil people — perhaps even more so than the Canaanite.

Ibn Ezra, in his commentary on the Torah, associates the nation of the Perizzite with “Sidon,” the firstborn son of Canaan.

questions.title_en: Jew without Brit Milá: Can they wear Tefillin?
questions.question: Can a Jew born to a Jewish mother, who has not yet undergone Brit Milá (circumcision), put on Tefillin?

answers.text:
As mentioned in the comments, Teffilin is not one of the mitzvot that an uncircumcised person cannot fulfill. The following is the list of mitzvot that an uncircumcised person cannot fulfill (teffilin not being there):

  1. Korban Pesach- see Shemot 12:48

  2. Terumah- see Gemera in Yevamot 70a.

  3. Kodshim- see Rambam Maseh Korbanot 10:9

  4. Avodah in Beit Hamikdash- See Zevachim 22b

  5. Circumcising others- If the person didn't want to get a brit milah on purpose, then he can't circumcise others, see Yoreah Deah 2:7.

  6. Korban ראיה- see Chagigah 4b, and Rambam Hilchot Chagigah 2:1 (although this might be a bit different since it says פטור and not אסור).

7. Uncircumcised Kohen for Birkat Kohanim- see Bach O.C 128:44, שיירי כנסת הגדולה סימן קכח:כד, Pri Chadash 128:39, Pri Megadim 128 Eshel Avraham Seif Katan 54, Eliyah Rabah 128:69, and others.

8. Getting an aliyah- In the Minchat Yitzchak 4:10 he says not to give an uncircumcised person an aliyah; however, the Sridei Eish I:11 and Igrot Moshe 2:33 say it's allowed.

If I missed any please let me know, but the idea behind doing this is to show all the examples that an uncircumcised person cannot fulfill and how teffilin is not on the list.

questions.title_en: Sephardic Tefillin: One or Two Mitzvot?
questions.question: For Sephardic Jews, is the arm and head Tefillin considered a single mitzvah or two separate mitzvot? They recite one blessing for both, while Ashkenazi Jews recite a separate blessing for each Tefillin, from what I understand.

answers.text: The number of mitzvos do not change because someone made one or 2 blessings on tefilin. The source for making only one bracha to cover both is found in the talmud menachos 35b where it is explained you only make a second bracha on the shel rosh if one interrupted and spoke after putting on the shel yad. This is also brought down in the rambam hilchos tefilin chapter 4 halachos 4 and 5.

questions.title_en: What does Rashi mean "taryag mitzvos shamarti"?
questions.question:
In his message to Eisav in Bereishis 32:5, Yaakov says "עם לבן גרתי - I lived with Lavan," upon which Rashi famously says "עם לבן גרתי ותריג מצוות שמרתי - I lived with Lavan and I fulfilled the 613 mitzvos."

What does this mean? Best case scenario, he didn't fulfill all 613 mitzvos because no individual can, as many are designed for kohanim in the Bais Hamikdash. Furthermore, he married two sisters in direct violation of the Torah - and even if you argue that he wasn't obligated to keep the Torah because he was in Chutz La'aretz, he's still claiming to have done so!

questions.title_he: Meaning of הקריב in Bereshis 12:11
questions.question:
Rashi on Shemos 14:10 is troubled by the dikduk of ופרעה הקריב. If it meant that Pharaoh drew near, it would say קרב. The Hiphil form הקריב indicates that he caused someone to draw near. Rashi answers that he caused himself to draw near, that is, he pushed himself to lead the charge. (Elsewhere it's explained that he caused the Jews to become closer to Hashem.)

Bereshis 12:11, speaking of Avram's journey, seems to use a similar grammatical construction: ויהי כאשר הקריב לבוא מצרימה. Why doesn't Rashi take issue with the dikduk here? Shouldn't it say כאשר קרב?

answers.text:
Refer to the Perush Maharzu on Bereishis Rabbah 40:6

ויהי כאשר הקריב. פסוק זה מדבר בפרעה וזה צ"ע. שהרי עיקר הכוונה לדמות מעשה ישראל למעשה אברהם אך לא למעשה פרעה. אך לשון חכמים מרפא ומלמדנו דעת עומק הענינים. שהוקשה לחז"ל שהיל"ל כאשר קרב. על כן דורש אא"ע על קרבת המקום ת"ע על קרבת הלב שהרי לקיחת שרה לפרעה הוא אחד מיו"ד נסיונות. שאברם הבין וידע שתלקח שרה והקריב לבו ולבה להש"י על ידי פרעה ומצרים לבטוח בה' לעמוד בנסיון וזה סימן לישראל שנתקרבו ג"כ אל הש"י ע"י פרעה ומצרים אצל הים כמ"ש ופרעה הקריב ודרשו בשמ"ר פר' כ"א סימן ד' שהקריב לבן של ישראל לתשובה וזהו באמת הדמיון שאצל ישראל כתוב ופרעה הקריב ואצל אברהם כתוב כאשר הקריב. אחר זמן רב מצאתי כל זה מפורש בזוהר על פסוק זה כאשר הקריב ושמחתי כי כוונתי בדעת המדרש לאמתה של תורה. וז"ל הזוהר אר"א כאשר הקריב כאשר קרב מבעי ליה מאי כאשר הקריב אלא כדכתיב ופרעה הקריב דאיהו אקריב להו לישראל לתיובתא אוף הכי דאקריב גרמיה להקב"ה וכו': \nובישראל כתוב כל הבן. וס"ד וכל הבת תחיון: \nוייטב אלהים למילדות. והטובה היה מ"ש בסיפא וירב העם ויעצמו מאד הרי שהטובה לישראל: \nואברם כבד מאד במקנה. בכסף ובזהב לקמן פר' מ"א סוף סימן ב': \nויצו עליו פרעה. אנשים וישלחו אותו ובישראל כתיב ותחזק מצרים על העם למהר לשלחם מן הארץ ואין שילוח אלא לשון לויה כמ"ש במכילתא ריש בשלח ובשמ"ר פרשה כ

“And it came to pass, as he drew near…” – This verse speaks of Pharaoh, and this raises a question. For the primary intention is to compare the actions of Israel to those of Abraham, not to those of Pharaoh. However, the language of the Sages brings healing and teaches us the depth of matters.

The Sages were puzzled by the fact that the verse does not say “as he approached” (כַּאֲשֶׁר קָרַב), and therefore they interpreted it as referring to drawing near to the Omnipresent (God) – that is, drawing near with the heart. For the taking of Sarah by Pharaoh is one of the ten trials of Abraham. Abraham understood and knew that Sarah would be taken, and he offered his heart and hers to the Holy One, blessed be He, through Pharaoh and Egypt – to place their trust in God and withstand the test.

This serves as a sign for Israel, who also drew near to the Holy One, blessed be He, through Pharaoh and Egypt at the sea, as it is written: “And Pharaoh drew near” (וּפַרְעֹה הִקְרִיב). This is interpreted in Shemot Rabbah, Parashat 21, Section 4, to mean that Pharaoh brought the hearts of Israel closer to repentance.

This is the true parallel: in the case of Israel, it is written “And Pharaoh drew near,” and in the case of Abraham, it is written “as he drew near.”

After a long time, I found this very idea explicitly stated in the Zohar on this verse “as he drew near,” and I rejoiced, for my understanding of the Midrash aligned with the truth of the Torah.

And these are the words of the Zohar: Rabbi Elazar said, “‘As he drew near’ – it should have said ‘as he approached.’ Why does it say ‘as he drew near’? Rather, as it is written, ‘And Pharaoh drew near,’ meaning that he brought Israel near to repentance. So too, here, he brought himself closer to the Holy One, blessed be He,” etc.

questions.title_en: Numbers mi yodeya - how do we look at numbers in the Torah?
questions.question:
I recently disagreed with a friend on the following question. I wonder if others can bring evidence.

Assumed: For various numbers the Torah seems to treat the number as being significant. (See the Mi Yodeya series here on every number you've ever heard of.) For example, there are many "threes" (Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov; Pesach, Shavuos, Sukkos; Moshe, Aharon, Miriam;...) We seem to understand that there is some underlying idea that these "threes" share. The same is true for many examples of "fours", many examples of "tens", "forties", etc. Each number represents something shared by its examples; see the Maharal and many others who discuss what the underlying ideas are.

Question: Do we think that all the cases of "threes", say, should be matched up in a specific one-to-one way? So (as a Midrash says), Pesach is Avraham Avinu, Shavuos is Yitzchak, Sukkos is Yaakov. Or the Ten Makos in Mitzrayim match up with the Asarah Maamaros that created the world: see the Maharal who puts them in reverse order, and some Achronim who switch the order... As the examples show, sometimes that is a good idea. Is it always true?
Of course, it maybe be difficult or impractical to do it, above our level. But in theory, yes, you should be able to match up each "ten" one-to-one, and each "seventy", etc. That was my friend's position and he claimed his rabbeim would agree with him.

I thought that was absurd. לשבר את האוזן, just because something is a three-dimensional system, say, doesn't mean that there's only one way to choose the axes. Depending on where you're standing on the earth, Up/Down, Forward/Back, Left/Right can be completely different directions - all perfectly acceptable and all very different and independent. My "up" can be equal to a sum of parts of your "up, back, and left". Why should Moshe, Aharon, and Miriam have to represent the same three sides as Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov do? Maybe they're three different kinds of side.
Do you really think that the seventy souls who went down to Mitzrayim, just because they correspond to the seventy nations, have to match up one by one? Which one is Kush and which one gets to be Peleg? Which of the seventy nations is from the side of Leah, and which from the side of Rachel or Bilhah? I'm not saying it's hard to decide. I'm asking why you're so sure that exactly one of them corresponds to exactly one of the other group. Maybe it's just the aspect of "seventy" that they share, along with the Sanhedrin, along with the Parim on Sukkos, but they represent very different ways of looking at that aspect.

Anyhow, does someone discuss this?

questions.title_en: Kayin, Hevel, Yaval, Yuval, Tuval-Kayin & Keinan
questions.question:
I find interesting that in the aftermath of Hevel's murder by Kayin, several characters in Bereshit perek 4 and 5 seem to share either partially, fully or a combination of Hevel or Kayin's names.

Do Yaval, Yuval and Tuval share the same root name as Hevel? If yes, what would be the significance of it?

answers.text:
Rabbi Ahron Marcus in his commentary on Tanach (of which only the beginning of Beresheet was printed and hence survived the Holocaust), Keset Ha'Sofer, Beresheet 4:20 (new edition, p. 212; can be found on Otzar Hachochmah]) stated that the name "Hevel" means "son",1 and that all three of Lemech's sons' names - Yaval, Yuval, Tuval-Kayin - are connected to that root.

Regarding the significance of the similarities between the names, Ariel Feiglin, "For the Secret of Man (Adam) and Land (Adamah) - Between Adam & Kayin and the Commandments of the First Fruits and the Decapitated Calf" (בסוד אדם ואדמה - בין אדם וקין למצוות ביכורים ועגלה ערופה), Asif 5 (5778), p. 111 suggested that Kayin and his family attempted to make amends for the murder of Hevel via two fronts: Kayin built a city - Chanoch - which intended to fix the socio-international aspect of the world (building instead of destroying/killing), while his descendant Lemech named his sons after Hevel - intended to fix the personal-familial aspect of the world. Lemech also preserved Hevel's memory by marrying two women, as according to a midrash that one daughter was born with Kayin and two with Hevel.

Each of the three sons went on to amend Hevel's death in his own way: Yaval took up Hevel's mantle as a shepherd, and Yuval created music which is connected to the same pastoral lifestyle, and is also connected to Ruach Hakodesh (see Melachim 2:3:15), reflecting Hevel's closeness to Hashem. Tuval-Kayin is more complicated. He reflects a merge of Hevel and Kayin - he is named after Hevel like his brothers, but also after Kayin. He invented metal weapons that could be used to kill - detrimental to the world's development.2 His actions led to the killing of Kayin by Lemech (see Rashi on Beresheet 4:24). This necessitated the killing of Tuval-Kayin by Lemech, as justice. This reflects the completion of the seven-generations-long justice process for Hevel's murder.

Regarding Keinan, Rabbi Marcus, Keset, p. 220 suggested that it is an unrelated name that comes from Hebrew קינה, referring to the tragic event that took place during his father (Enosh)'s lifetime: The double flooding of the world (Beresheet Rabbah 23:7).

1 In his book on the development of the Hebrew language, Barzilai (Hebrew translation, can be found on Otzar Hachochmah), pp. 126-127, Rabbi Marcus clarified that "Hevel" comes from a Mesopotamian word, the Akkadian ablu, which had been proposed as a possible etymology for Hevel in the 19th century.

2 "Kayin" is a word that is also related to metallurgy. See some sources here. This was also noted by Rabbi Marcus in Keset, p. 212.

questions.title_en: Is G.od the exclusive creator of life?
questions.question:
In “The Religious Implications of Extraterrestrial Life” (first published in Tradition 7/8 [1965–66] and reprinted in Challenge, p. 396 n.31), Rabbi Norman Lamm suggests that Judaism does not require belief in God as the exclusive Creator of life.

Lamm (pp. 36 - 42), discussing the scientific possibility of lab made life states that the creation of life ex materia is not a contradiction to Judaism:

There is no fundamental of the Jewish faith that for its own dogmatic integrity, requires or implies the belief that God is the exclusive Creator of life.

Is Lamm correct in implying that Jewish faith does not necessitate belief in God as the exclusive Creator of life?

answers.text:
The Ramban clearly believes that God has partners in creation. Commentary to Genesis 1:26

The correct explanation of na’aseh (let us make) [which is in the plural form when it should have been in the singular] is as follows: It has been shown to you that G-d created something from nothing only on the first day, and afterwards He formed and made things from those created elements. Thus when He gave the waters the power of bringing forth a living soul, the command concerning them was Let the waters swarm. The command concerning cattle was Let the earth bring forth. But in the case of man He said, Let us make, that is, I and the aforementioned earth, let us make man, the earth to bring forth the body from its elements as it did with cattle and beasts, as it is written, And the Eternal G-d formed man of the dust of the ground, and He, blessed be He, to give the spirit from His mouth, the Supreme One, as it is written, And He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. And He said, In our image, and after our likeness, as man will then be similar to both. In the capacity of his body, he will be similar to the earth from which he was taken, and in spirit he will be similar to the higher beings, because it [the spirit] is not a body and will not die. In the second verse, He says, In the image of G-d He created him, in order to relate the distinction by which man is distinguished from the rest of created beings. The explanation of this verse I have found ascribed to Rabbi Joseph the Kimchite, and is the most acceptable of all interpretations that have been advanced concerning it.

questions.title_en: Permissible Hefsek while reading The Megillah
questions.question:
I wish to present a halachic inquiry regarding the reading of the Megillah, specifically regarding the practice of making certain verbal additions during the kriyah itself.

Specifically, I am curious whether there is room to permit the inclusion of the phrase “חרבונה זכור לטוב” within the reading, as mentioned by Rav Pinchas and others. We find this concept already in the Yerushalmi (Megillah 3:7), which describes that Rabbi Yonasan, upon reaching the verse mentioning Nevuchadnezzar, would pause and declare: “נבוכדנצר שחיק עצמות.”

The Gemara proceeds to ask why this was not similarly done when reading Nevuchadnezzar’s name in Yirmiyahu — clarifying that such an addition was made during the reading itself and not afterward.

This theme reappears in Bereishis Rabbah (49): רַבִּי בֶּרֶכְיָה וְרַבִּי חֶלְבּוֹ מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָן וְרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן... רַב כִּי הֲוָה מָטֵי לְהָמָן בְּפוּרִים, אָמַר אָרוּר הָמָן וַאֲרוּרִים בָּנָיו... אָמַר רַבִּי פִּינְחָס חַרְבוֹנָה זָכוּר לַטּוֹב.

The Matnas Kehunah there explains explicitly that Rav Pinchas made this declaration as he reached the verse mentioning Charvonah during his reading of the megillah: א"ר פנחס... בפורים כשהגיע לפסוק ויאמר חרבונה.

The Maharzu suggests alternatively that perhaps these expressions were said after the completion of the Megillah, to avoid any appearance of a hefsek between the berachos and the mitzvah of reading: ...אך במס' סופרים איתא בהדיא שרב אמר כן אחר קריאת המגילה... אפשר שהטעם משום הפסק הברכה והמ"ע יקיים אחר הקריאה.

Moving forward in time, the Shulchan Aruch (O.C. 690:16) codifies that one should say: צריך שיאמר ארור המן ברוך מרדכי... וצריך שיאמר וגם חרבונה זכור לטוב,

which seems to legitimize such additions as part of the reading experience itself.

Nevertheless, later authorities such as Peninei Halacha — and this appears to reflect the common custom — specify that these statements are recited after the Megillah reading: צריך לומר אחר הקריאה... וגם חרבונא זכור לטוב.

However, it would seem from other sources — including Shulchan Aruch O.C. 690:13, Yerushalmi Megillah 2:2, and Mishnah Berurah 690:19 — that a brief verbal interjection of this nature would not constitute a hefsek invalidating the reading. These sources indicate that not every interruption or reaction during the reading rises to the level of a prohibited hefsek, especially where it is derech kavod or derech mitzvah, as would be the case here.

Having reviewed these sources, my main question is as follows:

Is it halachically permissible, in principle, to make such additions during the reading of the Megillah itself — such as saying “חרבונה זכור לטוב” aloud upon reaching that verse — or would this nonetheless be considered an invalidating hefsek? Additionally, if this is permissible, would the same apply equally to a private reading (for oneself or one’s family) as to a public congregational reading?

answers.text:
There is a discussion in the poskim with regards to saying ושם רשעים ירקב (pasuk in Mishlei 10:7) when getting to המן, which we would then apply to all other phrases mentioned in Masechet Sofrim 14:6 and other places.

The Magen Avraham 690:21 citing the Levush, the Shalmei Tzibur page 328, Chemdat Yamim Purim Perek 3, Hagahot Uminhagim Purim אות נה, permit to say ושם רשעים ירקב (Mishlei 10:7).

In Sefer Shenot Chaim Siman 32 footnote 16, Kaf Hachaim 690:11, Chazon Ovadia Purim page 93 forbid saying it.

What's the possible reason for both sides?

Side that permits it: Sha'ar hatziun 690:57 writes that it's not a hefsek based on Shulchan Aruch O.C 690:13; however there could be a big problem where if people start saying ושם רשעים ירקב every time Haman is mentioned, there will be many who won't be able to hear the words before or after Haman, which is a big problem. However, Rav Moshe in Igrot Moshe Orach Chaim 1:192 says that even if we use this Shulchan Aruch to permit saying ושם רשעים ירקב after every Haman, this is not a lechatchila thing to do, even though it's technically valid, since maybe in the case of the Shulchan Aruch, the guy never said a bracha before the meggilah reading. And the Tosfoat in Brachot 13a in the name of the Yerushalmi says that Brachot are not מעכב, and Tosfoat Brachot 14a says that by Hallel for Rosh Chodesh, if one doesn't say a bracha, it's not שייך to say that there is a הפסק. Furthermore, that Yerushalmi Meggilah 3:7 that Rebbi Yonatan said נבוכדנצר שחיק עצמות might have been during the reading itself, therefore the Yerushalmi says there is no הפסק, if you learn like that. Furthermore, maybe based on the Midrash in Yalkut Parashat Vayera, 82, it says that anyone who mentions a bad guy and doesn't curse him goes over a לאו. The proofs that one should do this even while reading the meggilah would be from the Midrashim (Ester Rabah פרשה י, Beresheit Rabah Vayeira פרשה מט, and Yerushalmi meggilah 3:7.

Side that doesn't permit it: Rav Moshe then concludes that the Rosh Meggilah 1:8 says that this saying was after kriat hameggilah, and Rebbi Yonatan just did it as he was learning the meggilah in depth. Therefore, because of a safek it is better not to say the phrase. In Chazon Ovadia Purim page 93 he brings in the argument that people might still not be able to hear the words before and after Haman which be very problematic.

Conclusion: From the Rav Moshe and Rav Ovadia in Chazon Ovadia Purim Page 93 and others, it seems that this should not be done lechatchilah (even though its technically permissible according to halacha) mainly because people might miss the words of the meggilah thus causing people to not fulfill the mitzvah.

I would think that even if the meggilah is being read for ones family it would still be a problem based on the reason that people might still not be able to hear the words before and after Haman, however if someone is reading it to themselves, then there would be no problem seemingly.

questions.title_en: Why did these gedolim seemingly regularly not daven with minyan for sake of focused intense learning?
questions.question:
I know of two Gedolim who apparently went into "seclusion mode" in their youth in order to learn Torah. Interestingly, they both went to a hut by a river.

  • The first is the Arizal, who did so when he started learning the Zohar and developing his system (source: Wikipedia). He only came home for Shabbat.

  • The second is the Bava Sali z'tl (I think! Maybe it was HaRav Kaduri z'tl), who also did this when he was younger. I can't remember which biography I saw this in.

I am assuming they both missed minyan during the week at those times. There are other examples of Gedolim missing minyan regularly:

  • The Chafetz Chaim z'tl would sometimes miss minyan (mincha and/or maariv) when writing his sefarim. See here: Chafetz Chaim and Maariv (thanks @JoelK)

  • The Lubavitcher Rebbe z'tl would daven Shacharis alone in his room throughout the year. See this Derher edition, first page. (Thanks @TheTargum)

Can someone explain the circumstances that they were seemingly able to do this? Was this halachically sound, and if so how? What is the precedent and how can one know if and when one should do the same?

Note: I'd prefer to avoid halachic politics. If some say they had precedent for this, and others say actually no, they had no precedent and those who say so are wrong, I'd rather not get into that. I'd rather hear from those who say they had precedent and how. We can ask another question about whether that's legitimate or not.

answers.text:
Three possible theories:

  1. Rabbeinu Yonah on the Rif Berachot 4a brings the opinion of the rabbonim of France that one need not leave one's place of learning in order to pray in a minyan because it is better to pray alone in a place designated for the study of Torah day and night than to pray in a shul in a minyan. So maybe that’s what the Arizal and others relied on.

  2. The Rema Orach Chaim Siman 90:18 (quoting Rishonim) says that someone for whom תורתו אומנתו (whose learning is his “occupation”), meaning that one does not waste any time not learning except for the absolutely necessary activities, may daven without being part of a minyan; however, nowadays this is discouraged. So perhaps the Arizal and others also relied on this.

  3. Piskei Teshuvot O.C 90:9 quotes the Pri Megadim Siman 101 Mishbetzot Zahav Seif Katan 1, and also brought in the Biur Halacha that says one is permitted to daven by himself if he is, גדול הדור ומפורסם שכל מעשיו לשם שמים, which could be someone like the Arizal and Baba Sali. In the Mishmeret Shalom 10:4 he says that those who want to have the kavvanot of the Arizal (which are long and require lots of concentration and no distractions) may daven themselves, so this may also explain the practice of the Arizal and Baba Sali (who was also a very big kabbalist).

questions.title_en: What is the source for the connection between Avraham Avinu and chalitza mentioned in the Seder Chalitza in Shulchan Aruch?
questions.question:
In the Seder Hachalitza as found in the back of Shulchan Oruch Even Ha’ezer, the Mechaber writes that:

Sefaria Link

מצאתי כתוב בסדר אשכנז וכשיעמדו יאמר הרב בא"י אמ"ה אקב"ו במצות וחוקים של אברהם אבינו והטעם מדאמרינן בפרק כיסוי דם בשכר שאמר אברהם ועד שרוך נעל זכו בניו למנעל של חליצה ויש לאומרו בלא הזכרת שם ומלכות:

translation: I found it written in an Ashkenazi order of service: When they stand, the rabbi should say: "Blessed are You, Hashem, our God, King of the Universe, Who has sanctified us with the commandments and statutes of Avraham our father." And the reason is that we say (in Tractate Chullin, Chapter Kisuy HaDam) that in reward for Avraham saying “from a thread to a sandal strap” (Bereishit 14:23), his descendants merited the shoe used in the act of chalitzah. And it may be said without mentioning the Divine Name and Kingship (i.e., omitting “Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the Universe”).

So far as I can tell, however, the gemara in Chullin (89a; and this is also in Sota 17a) says that זכו בניו לשתי מצות לחוט של תכלת ורצועה של תפילין ("his children merited two mitzvot, the thread blue in tsitsis and the strap of tefillin") but there is nothing there about חליצה.

So, does anyone know of a source for this reference in the Shulchan Aruch?
